answer.label: In short
answer.lead: Contribution margin is what is left of an order's revenue after the costs that come with that order, and break-even ROAS is the ROAS at which ad spend uses up exactly that amount.

paras: Contribution margin is the money an order leaves behind after the costs that vary with that order. For a D2C brand these are product cost, packaging, shipping, payment gateway fees and the cost of returns. Rent, salaries and software are fixed costs and sit outside it.
It matters because it is the pool your advertising has to be paid from. Whatever an order leaves behind before ads is the most you can spend to win that order and still break even.

callout.title: The short version
callout.text: Contribution margin before ads, as a share of revenue, sets your break-even ROAS. Break-even ROAS is 1 divided by that share.

blocks.h: Why revenue and platform ROAS mislead
paras: ROAS divides the revenue an ad platform reports by what you spent on ads. It says nothing about what it cost to make and deliver those orders. Two stores can both report the same ROAS and one can be profitable while the other loses money on every sale.
Also check whether the revenue in your ROAS includes tax. Compare like with like: use the same basis for the ROAS you read and the margin you calculate.

blocks.h: How to work it out, step by step

steps.d: Use the average order value, before tax if your costs are before tax.
What it costs you to buy or make the items in that order.
Include the forward shipping you pay, and cash-on-delivery handling if you offer it.
Gateway and collection charges on the order.
The average cost of returns and failed deliveries, spread across all orders.

steps.t: Divide what is left by the order value
steps.d: That is your contribution margin before ads. Divide 1 by it to get break-even ROAS.

callout.title: What that gives
callout.text: Contribution before ads is 50% of order value, so break-even ROAS is 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2.0. Break-even cost per order is ₹500. A campaign at ROAS 3.0 leaves margin after ads. A campaign at ROAS 1.8 loses money even though it looks healthy.

blocks.h: Why returns and failed deliveries change the answer
paras: A returned or refused order earns nothing but still costs shipping, often both ways, plus packaging and handling. For brands that ship cash on delivery, this can move break-even ROAS by a full point or more.
That is why the returns allowance is its own line. If you do not include it, your break-even ROAS looks lower than it really is, and campaigns look safer than they are.
blocks.cap: Returned parcels are a cost that ad dashboards do not show.

list: Set a floor: campaigns below break-even ROAS need a fix or a pause, unless they are bringing customers who reorder.
Set a target above it: the gap between your ROAS and break-even is the margin your ads leave.
Change it when your costs change: a price rise, a cheaper courier or lower returns all move break-even ROAS.
Read repeat customers separately. A first order that only breaks even can still pay off if the customer comes back. See the LTV:CAC calculator.

blocks.h: Work it out with your own numbers
paras: The break-even ROAS calculator does the sums above with your costs, and the unit economics calculator scales one order into a monthly profit and loss. Both are free to use.
If you would like a senior strategist to read your figures with you, bring them to the audit call.
